raw_case_text:
The team was informed that the rapid diagnostic stool test for the patient's daughter, who was 31 years old, was positive. As every family member denied suffering any symptoms on the first field visit, another visit was conducted to further investigate the possibility of a secondary case in the family. On interviewing the patient at her home, although she looked well and was not dehydrated, she confirmed that she had begun to experience frequent loose bowel movements and moderate to severe abdominal pain on April 26, and that she had sought medical consultation at a nearby health center, where she was given supportive treatment and discharged. When asked why she had not reported this to the public health team, she answered that she thought her symptoms were irrelevant to her father's condition. The patient was then given a 300 mg stat dose of doxycycline along with hyoscine butyl bromide. She was advised to use a designated toilet, and the need for strict hand washing was emphasised. In 2 more days, the patient's condition had improved, and her symptoms had disappeared. Her culture report was released on May 1; this also showed growth of a similar isolate of her father, V. cholerae O1 E1 Tor, subtype Inaba, fully sensitive to ampicillin, chloramphenicol, tetracycline, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. Figure 1 presents an overview of the 2 patients' clinical progress, the tests performed, and their management.
The initial workup of the stool samples in the regional hospital laboratory revealed a Gram-negative non-lactose-fermenter coccobacilli curved shape. The stool samples analysed in the regional hospital laboratory were positive on the rapid cholera antigen test. Stool samples were cultured and the growing isolates were sent to the Central Public Health Laboratory (CPHL) on MacConkey agar for identification and confirmation, susceptibility testing, and serotyping. At the CPHL, the isolates were sub-cultured on blood agar and thiosulfate-citrate-bile-salts-sucrose agar and incubated in air at 35-37 C for 18-24 hours. Fermentation of sugars such as glucose, maltose, mannitol, and sucrose tested positive using the Vitek system (Vitek-2 Compact; bioMerieux, Marcy-l'Etoile, France). Most strains were also motile at 37 C, metabolized lysine and ornithine, and showed a positive string test. The isolates were identified using a matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization biotyper (Bruker, Billerica, MA, USA), which indicated that the bacteria were a Vibrio species. Vitek was used for identification and it gave a 98% probability that the isolates were V. cholerae.
The agglutination test (V. cholerae antisera) used was positive for V. cholerae serogroup O1 serovar Inaba. Since the growth showed haemolysis of colonies, the strain was most probably El Tor V. cholerae. Antibiotic susceptibility testing was done using disc diffusion for ampicillin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole according to the relevant guidelines (M100, 29th edition, Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute).
Written informed consent was obtained from the patient for publication of this case report and any accompanying images.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 31-year-old female presenting with frequent loose stools and moderate-to-severe abdominal pain for approximately 1 day.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient is the daughter of an index patient hospitalized with severe acute gastrointestinal illness. Following her father's return from Pakistan, she directly assisted with cleaning his vomitus and oral secretions from his mouth and body without protective equipment. She subsequently developed frequent loose bowel movements and moderate to severe abdominal pain on April 26, 2019. She sought outpatient evaluation at a local health center where supportive care was given. During secondary household contact tracing following an initial positive stool screening test, she confirmed active gastrointestinal symptoms.
subjective.past_medical_history: Household secondary contact of an index case with severe acute diarrheal illness; directly handled and cleaned infectious vomitus and oral secretions without protective measures. No prior chronic illnesses documented.
subjective.review_of_systems: Frequent loose bowel movements, moderate to severe abdominal pain; denies vomiting, fever, or hematochezia.

objective.physical_examination: Clinically well-appearing, hydrated, no signs of dehydration or systemic instability.
objective.advanced_workup: Antimicrobial susceptibility testing via disc diffusion (CLSI M100, 29th edition): isolate fully sensitive to ampicillin, tetracycline, chloramphenicol, and trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Definitive diagnosis of secondary cholera transmission due to Vibrio cholerae serogroup O1 biovar El Tor, serotype Inaba: Stool rapid diagnostic antigen dipstick (Crystal VC) was positive; stool culture grew curved Gram-negative non-lactose-fermenting coccobacilli on MacConkey agar; subculture on TCBS agar grew yellow sucrose-fermenting colonies and blood agar revealed colonies with hemodigestion; motile at 37 C, positive string test, metabolized lysine and ornithine; Vitek-2 Compact confirmed glucose, maltose, mannitol, and sucrose fermentation (98% probability V. cholerae); Bruker MALDI-TOF biotyper confirmed Vibrio species; slide agglutination confirmed V. cholerae serogroup O1 serovar Inaba. Antimicrobial therapy: Oral doxycycline 300 mg single stat dose along with oral hyoscine butylbromide for abdominal cramps. Advised on strict enteric precautions, dedicated toilet use, and meticulous hand hygiene. Symptoms completely resolved within 48 hours.
